newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania sacks army chief over arms looting.
newsitem.headline: Albania sacks army chief over arms looting.

text.p: Albanian authorities said on Wednesday that army chief of staff General Sheme Kosova had been dismissed and replaced by Major General Adem Copani, President Sali Berisha's personal military adviser.

A statement from the prime minister's office published in the newspaper Rilindja Demokratike said Kosova had been sacked for failing to ensure adequate security at military posts stormed and looted of their weapons by "terrorists".

Albania's parliament, controlled by Berisha's Democratic Party, declared a national state of emergency on Sunday after an armed uprising in the south of the former Stalinist state, Europe's poorest country.

Rioters stormed army and police weapons depots and seized their arms and ammunition. The embattled authorities said on Tuesday that what they call "red rebels" remained in control of the Adriatic port of Vlore and the coastal town of Sarande.

Kosova was relieved of his duties because of "insufficient security measures...which resulted in military installations being destroyed and a considerable quantity of weapons and ammunition being looted by terrorists," the statement said.
A defence ministry statement said Kosova had been replaced by Copani. Neither said whether Kosova had been arrested. They were issued after unconfirmed reports of the sacking on Tuesday.
The government has sent soldiers, police and other security forces south from the capital Tirana in a push to restore order.

Albanian television on Tuesday showed foreign television film of tanks on a road near Gjirokaster, Albania's main southern town near the Greek border. Foreign journalists have seen tanks moving south from Tirana on flatbed trucks.
The defence ministry also said on Wednesday that the air force was making reconnaissance flights over the area but denied pilots had orders to shoot on civilians.

It issued the statement after two pilots who flew their MiG plane to southern Italy on Tuesday and asked for political asylum told Italian reporters that they defected rather than follow orders to fire on demonstrators near Gjirokaster.
"These declarations are totally untrue," the statement said.

More than 20 people have been reported killed since last Friday in southern flashpoint towns, where unrest that began two months ago over the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes has mushroomed into an anti-government uprising.
Many members of the military, like other Albanians, lost savings in the collapse of the "get-rich-quick" funds.
Several cases were reported over the weekend of army commanders and ordinary soldiers abandoning their posts without a shot after they were stormed by rioters.
One senior Democratic Party source said on Monday that the behaviour by some commanders had been a "disgrace".
Berisha has blamed the unrest on the opposition Socialist Party and members of the former communist elite.
Rilindja Demokratike, the Berisha party newspaper, said on Tuesday that military prosecutors were investigating cases of suspected dereliction of duty.
Soldiers and officers "of all ranks" against whom there was evidence would be put on trial and risked stern punishment, it said.
